data.title: Health insurance plan costs on Healthcare.gov to rise by double digits in 2027
data.description:
Obamacare enrollees could see their health insurance premiums rise by double digits for a second year in a row, according to a report published Friday.

Health research group KFF found the average cost of Obamacare health insurance will rise by 13 percent in 2027, following a 26 percent hike in rates from 2025 to 2026.

KFF made these calculations was based on new data the Trump administration shared earlier in the day, which listed 2027 prices for the 30 states with federal health insurance marketplaces. These new rates came ahead of the opening of the 2027 enrollment period on Sunday. 

Around 19.2 million Americans are enrolled in Obamacare plans, according to an estimate from the federal government earlier this year. A KFF analysis from May found that enrollment in this program fell in 2026 after four consecutive years of record growth. 

President Trump’s administration has implemented new barriers to enrolling in these programs as part of its efforts to crackdown on alleged widespread fraud. Earlier this year, Obamacare’s enhanced premium tax subsidies expired after Republican lawmakers opposed a Democrat-led push to extend them. 

Under the first Trump administration, Obamacare premium costs rose by an average of 20 percent in 2017 and 34 percent in 2018, according to KFF’s analysis. 

The estimated Obamacare premium cost increases for 2027 are similar to changes anticipated in other health insurance increases programs, with federal and employer plans expected to increase by around 10 percent in this timeframe. 

Health care costs have become a key issue in the midterm elections, as the rising cost of living continues to poll highest among the top concerns motivating Americans’ votes in this election. 

A KFF survey published earlier this month found six in 10 voters said they were concerned about being able to afford their health insurance and out-of-pocket medical bills. Respondents ranked health care costs on par with gas prices as the most important affordability issue this election cycle. 

The Trump administration has sought to address these concerns ahead of Election Day. The president announced the federal government would disburse one-time $500 checks to nearly 1 million Americans the administration said were overcharged for Obamacare.

Earlier this month, the administration also began sending out $90 each to over 20 million seniors enrolled in Medicare Part B — totaling around $2 billion. 

Democrats have vowed to make restoring Obamacare subsidies and health care tax credits a top issue if they regain control of Congress.

The Big Story 

Ukraine gets approval for Patriot missile sale

The State Department approved on Friday a possible $2.1 billion sale of 500 Patriot interceptor missiles to Ukraine that is funded entirely by U.S. partners and allies. 

© Getty

The Trump administration greenlit the sale of 500 PATRIOT Advanced Capability-3 (PAC-3) Missile Segment Enhancement (MSE) missiles, including classified and unclassified spare parts

 

“This proposed sale will support the foreign policy and national security objectives of the United States by improving the security of a partner country that is a force for political and economic stability in Europe,” the State Department said in the press release. 

 

Ukraine will pay for the purchase with donations from Norway, Germany and Canada via the JUMPSTART program and national funds. No U.S. funds are involved in the transaction. 

 

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has said that Patriot missile interceptors are paramount to shooting down Russian missiles and drones targeting the country’s cities. 

 

Zelensky has previously accused the Pentagon of delaying deliveries of missile interceptors that other nations bought for Kyiv. 

 

“We have been waiting for nearly a month for Mr. Hegseth to sign off on missiles for Patriots and NASAMS,” Zelensky said this week. 

 

Two weeks ago, Hegseth told reporters that the Pentagon has not changed its posture toward Ukraine, but noted that “we want to make sure our guys have the most possible” interceptors.

The Big Story 

Trump says Iran war will end ‘soon’

President Trump claimed on Friday that the U.S. war against Iran will end “soon” as he mulls authorizing military strikes on the Islamic Republic following the November midterm elections. 

© Jon Cherry, Associated Press

Note to readers: This newsletter should have showed up in your inbox last night. Our apologies. We’re back to regularly scheduled programming this evening. 

 

“It’s going to get wrapped up soon,” the president said in ‌an ⁠interview Friday morning with Kansas-based radio station KCMO. “We need a guarantee there’ll never ⁠be a nuclear weapon.”

 

The president reiterated during the interview that the U.S. military will not conduct strikes against Iran before the next week’s midterm elections. 

 

The war, which began in late February, is nearing its eight month as the cost of the conflict has risen to $47 billion, according to the Pentagon. 

 

Trump’s comments come as Iran has not yet responded to a letter Vice President Vance sent last week to the Iranian Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei, according to Tasnim News Agency, a semi-official Iranian news agency linked with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

 

The U.S. Central Command (Centcom) has drawn up multiple Iranian strike options, which could be exercised after the midterms if there is authorization from the White House, The Hill previously reported. 

 

Centcom Commander Adm. Brad Cooper said in a video posted on Friday that Iran’s navy is decimated and that southern shipping routes in the Strait of Hormuz are open.

 

Cooper’s remarks come as Iran claimed that six commercial ships struck sea mines in the waterway in recent days.

data.title: RNC chair predicts GOP wins in Alaska, Texas, 3 other battlegrounds
data.description:
Republican National Committee (RNC) Chair Joe Gruters remained optimistic Friday evening about his party’s chances in next week’s midterms, predicting big wins in key battleground states despite troubling polling numbers for the GOP.

Gruters told NewsNation’s Blake Burman he expects Republicans will win Senate races in Maine, Texas, Ohio and Alaska — all of which The Hill’s nonpartisan election forecasting partner, Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), lean “narrowly” toward Democrats. He also predicted a GOP victory in North Carolina, which the handicapper says will “likely” go blue.

Burman pressed the RNC chair on generic ballot polling that displayed a disadvantage for Republicans running this election cycle. An Emerson College Polling survey released Friday found Democrats held a 10-point lead over Republicans on a generic ballot.  

“We put up candidates that can win and common-sense mainstream candidates, and I think that will make the difference,” Gruters told Burman. “So yes, maybe the generic ballot, we’re not doing so hot, but when it comes to candidates that are well known and they’re getting their message out, yes, we do have the benefit.”

DDHQ places the Democrats’ chances of regaining control of the House this November at 82 percent, according to a Friday forecast. The party has a slimmer chance at retaking the upper chamber of Congress, with the nonpartisan election handicapper placing this probability at around 62 percent. 

The RNC chair also addressed President Trump’s reversal on his decision to cancel two rallies set for this weekend in Iowa and Kansas. The president announced Friday the events were back on and will both be held in person on Sunday. 

“Listen, all these decisions are being made in real time,” Gruters said. “I mean, we’re looking at data, looking at where we may need to help certain candidates and people, and so there may be some more changes.”

Gruters also weighed in on Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy’s (R) response to reports that Democratic nominee Mary Peltola’s campaign was involved in an effort to recruit a candidate in the state’s Senate race with the same name as incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R).

When asked by Burman whether the RNC would seek to stall the certification of this election if Peltola was successful, Gruters said he would “follow the governor’s lead.”

“We’ll see [where] that investigation ends up, but we’re going to be ready to help any way we can,” he said.

On Friday, the top federal prosecutor in Alaska announced his office was involved in a separate investigation into whether any laws were broken in this alleged spoiler candidate effort. Peltola and her campaign have denied any involvement in the candidate’s recruitment.

data.title: Democrats weigh Israel election results amid lingering uncertainty
data.description:
The results of Israel’s elections this week have left Democrats on Capitol Hill with a mixed bag of emotions. 

The lawmakers say they’re heartened by the massive voter turnout, the erosion of support for conservative Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, and the potential influence of his top opponent, retired Gen. Gadi Eisenkot, over whatever governing coalition is ultimately formed. 

Eisenkot is seen as a more moderate figure when it comes to Israeli-Palestinian relations, to include his vows to rein in Israeli settler violence in the West Bank — a position that aligns him with Democrats in the Capitol. 

“I hope it bodes well for a coalition, a governing coalition, who reject some of what I find are the most grievous errors of Netanyahu’s time,” Rep. Madeleine Dean (D-Pa.), a senior member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said Friday by phone. 

But the Democrats are also anxious about the lingering uncertainty surrounding the results, after all parties fell short of the 61 seats needed to lead the Knesset. And they’re voicing concerns about the stark national divisions reflected by the election, which was broadly viewed as a referendum on Netanyahu’s leadership in the wake of the Oct. 7, 2023, massacre against Israelis by Hamas terrorists.  

“One of the signs is that there’s anything but unity in Israel, and so where do they go from here?” Rep. Brad Schneider (D-Ill.), one of Israel’s most vocal congressional allies, said Friday, also in a phone interview. “Only time will tell.”

Schneider characterized Eisenkot as a more reasonable partner, citing his commitment to curbing West Bank violence by Israeli settlers. 

“What they are doing is a threat to peace, and I think Eisenkot is more committed to thwarting that, and squashing it,” Schneider said. “That’s a critical thing.” 

Still, Eisenkot is no liberal. And progressive Democrats are worried that, despite Eisenkot’s break from Netanyahu on issues like settler violence and the need for a deeper investigation into the Oct. 7 attack, both candidates oppose the creation of a Palestinian state — a development many Democrats consider to be a crucial part of any lasting peace deal in the region. 

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) has repeatedly advocated for an autonomous Palestinian state as the only path to a long-term peace accord. His influence over the debate in Washington, D.C., is expected to grow tremendously, since Democrats are favored to control the House next year and Jeffries is in line to take the Speaker’s gavel. 

Already, he’s promising to stage a vote on legislation to apply economic sanctions on anyone who engages in violence in the occupied West Bank, while barring them from entering the U.S. The bill has been sponsored by 175 House Democrats.

Dean is one of them. And she said the party should “absolutely” pass the bill if they control the House next year. 

“America needs to lead,” she said. “We need to have our voices heard, and we can’t count on [Israeli leaders]. We have to have some moral courage and authority to say, ‘No more.’ 

“This is a series of wrongs, including killing, that we must absolutely, loudly, condemn.”

Tuesday’s election in Israel was the first since the attack of Oct. 7, when Hamas militants operating out of Gaza killed roughly 1,200 people and kidnapped 250 more.

The final results, unveiled Friday, left Netanyahu’s coalition with 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, while Eisenkot’s bloc held 48 seats and a group of Arab parties won 19. 

Democrats were quick to cheer the erosion of Netanyahu’s support, which fell from almost 70 seats before the elections. 

“That was the Israeli people saying, ‘We want something different,’” Schneider said. “No one in Israel wants to sacrifice their security — that’s true whether they’re Jewish or Muslim. They all want their kids to grow up in safety and security.”

“But I think they want a change in direction from this government, which is unquestionably the most extreme government in Israel’s history,” he added. “And you saw in the election a drift away from that.” 

What happens next remains unclear. The leaders of the various blocs are expected to huddle behind closed doors in an effort to forge some form of coalition that hits the 61-seat mark constituting a Knesset majority. The most likely scenarios include the formation of a unity government between the Netanyahu and Eisenkot blocs. 

Alternatively, Eisenkot’s group could join forces with the Arab parties, bonded by a shared opposition to Netanyahu.

If no such coalition can be built, Israel would stage another election.

In Washington, the Democrats’ approach to Israel relations is likely to be influenced by the composition of the governing coalition and how it addresses things like settler violence. 

“The actions the next government takes to address the extremist violence will most certainly affect how we look at either supporting the actions they’re taking, or putting pressure on [them] to take further action,” Schneider said. 

Dean, for her part, said she’s encouraged by the rising influence of the Arab parties, whose 19 seats in the Knesset is a new high mark. 

“What I do hope is, in these weeks and months coming up, more of the Arab voices and seats are heard and will change, will temper, whoever emerges as the leader,” she said.

The debate in Washington is also likely to be influenced by the incoming group of liberal lawmakers affiliated with the Democratic Socialists of America. Those lawmakers have been highly critical of Israel’s human rights record towards Palestinians, and they’re expected to bring their activism to Capitol Hill.

Dean said there’s been a broader attitudinal shift toward Israel in Congress since Netanyahu began attacking Gaza, which has led to the death of more than 70,000 people. She’s excited at the prospect of having more Netanyahu critics in the Capitol. 

“People were slow to separate Mr. Netanyahu from our love and support for Israel,” Dean said. “But I think we are well on our way, and I hope new members come in and help us make that argument in an even more robust way.”

data.title: Time to set back the clocks, much to Trump's chagrin
data.description:
Tick tock – clocks in America will fall back this Sunday. It could be the last time, if President Trump and some like-minded lawmakers get their way. But the debate over making daylight saving time permanent has proven divisive even within the president’s party. 

The House passed the Sunshine Protection Act earlier this year, which would end the semiannual clock change, but the Senate has yet to pick it up.

Trump has been a big proponent for the permanent change, slamming the Senate for “letting the Daylight Saving Bill die, when a vast Majority of the Country want it.”

“Most people are demanding light in the evening, but ALL want not to change their clocks anymore,” he wrote on Truth Social earlier this week. “TAKE A VOTE!”

Congress isn’t currently in session, and won’t be back until after the clocks change.

At his Mississippi rally on Monday, Trump called the clock change “ridiculous” and said it “drives everyone crazy, which nobody wants to do anymore.”

He pointed to data showing less crime is committed when there’s more light in the evening. Earlier this month, he argued the setback “costs our Country a fortune, is bad for Crime, stress on people, Sports, and just about everything else you can imagine.”

But voices on both sides of the debate can cite data proving their case. 

Rep. Mary Gary Scanlon (D-PA) and Rep. Pat Harrigan (R-NC) introduced bipartisan legislation in July called the Sunshine for Our Kids Act that would establish a permanent standard time (the current norm from November to March).

They worry more sunlight in the evenings leaves mornings dark for schoolchildren and commuters.

“For decades, scientists and medical professionals have highlighted the detrimental mental and physical health impacts of twice-a-year clock changes, particularly on children and teens,” Scanlon said in a statement. 

At least one Republican agrees with them: Sen. Tom Cotton (R-Ark.), typically a staunch Trump supporter. 

“No one likes changing the clock, me included, but Congress has enacted permanent Daylight Savings Time multiple times before and repealed it each time once Americans experienced absurdly late sunrises in the winter,” he wrote in a post on X earlier this month. “Arkansans don’t want their kids going to school in the pitch dark, and I’ll always put Arkansas first.”

An AP-NORC poll from last October found that 12 percent of U.S. adults favor the twice-a-year change, while 47 percent oppose it and 40 percent are indifferent about it.

Some 56 percent said they would prefer daylight saving time year-round, while 42 percent said they would rather standard daylight time year-round.

The golfing industry is a leading proponent of the argument that more daylight in the evenings is better for business – and the economy generally, with more people staying out after work and school.

“Overall, permanent DST is viewed as more beneficial to the golf industry, particularly for small business revenue, accessibility to the game, and general recreational enjoyment and benefits,” National Golf Course Owners Association CEO Jay Karen testified before a Senate committee last year. 

“Our industry is uniquely tied to daylight, and the number of playable hours directly affects the number of rounds we can offer, the staff we employ, and the revenue we generate, especially in the late afternoon and early evening.”

An analysis from JP Morgan Chase Institute found that in Los Angeles, when compared to a city like Phoenix that does not observe daylight saving, debit card spending per capita rose at the beginning of daylight saving by 0.9 percent. However, spending dropped 3.5 percent following the end of daylight saving time.

Andy Owen, the director of advocacy communications at the National Association of Convenience Stores, said the association doesn’t take an official position on permanent daylight saving time “although we would be comfortable with it.”

“Shifting daylight to the end of the day tends to be good for business because it provides more time for shopping after regular work hours,” he said. “We want what’s good for businesses.”

Studies do support Trump’s argument that crime and accidents occur less with permanent daylight saving time. One study found that full-year daylight saving would reduce pedestrian fatalities by 13 percent and motor vehicle occupant fatalities by 3 percent.

Similarly, research has found that robberies drop about 7 percent for the entire day and 27 percent during the evening hour when sunlight is gained.

David Bieri, an associate professor at Virginia Tech, put together a brief on which states would benefit the most and least if daylight saving time was made permanent.

He found that permanent daylight saving time would pay off more in the north and on the eastern side of the time zones, like Seattle, Boston and Chicago.

“Permanent daylight time’s safety case is strongest in places like Boston and weakest in places like Indianapolis,” he said.

And while Trump said the twice-a-year clock change is “stress on people,” health associations like the American Academy of Sleep Medicine, the American Medical Association and the Society for Research on Biological Rhythms all say standard daylight time is better for health than daylight saving time.

“There’s the immediate hit and then there’s the slow burn,” Dr. Carla Finkielston, a professor with Virginia Tech’s Fralin Biomedical Research Institute, said of the health effects linked to the time changes.

“In the first few days after the spring change, researchers have reported shorter sleep, worse performance, a bump in heart attacks compared with neighboring weeks, and possibly more traffic accidents,” she said. 

“The slow burn is the mismatch that sticks around, which we call social jetlag. Populations carrying more of that mismatch show higher rates of diabetes, obesity, heart disease, depression, and some cancers, along with shorter sleep and more trouble with mood and thinking.”

“The logic is simple enough. Standard Time is the arrangement where the clock on the wall sits closest to the sun overhead, so it asks the least of our biology,” she added.

While Trump has said the changing of the clocks is “a big inconvenience, and for our government, a VERY COSTLY EVENT,” studies have found that DST actually costs more.

Research from Chmura Economics & Analytics found that the total economic cost of DST in the U.S. is estimated at roughly $672.02 million annually, between lost productivity, injuries and accidents due to the sleep loss.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) doesn’t seem anxious to move on Trump’s daylight savings demands. He said earlier this month that there was no clear path for a successful vote on permanent daylight saving time in the Senate, despite the House passing the bill in a 308-117 vote.

Whether a Democratic majority would be inclined to make a change remains to be seen. 

“The clock is shared infrastructure — a public good like weights and measures,” Bieri said. “When the evidence is a coin toss, Washington shouldn’t pick the option that once again favours the places that already have the most.”

data.title: Feds 'intensely' probing alleged Alaska ballot scheme, US attorney confirms
data.description:
Federal authorities are investigating whether Democrat Mary Peltola campaign’s reported effort to recruit a candidate in the Alaska Senate race with the same name as incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R) violated the law, the state’s top federal prosecutor announced Friday.

U.S. Attorney for the District of Alaska Michael Heyman said during a press conference that this investigation has been in the works for several months but that federal authorities are looking into the matter “intensely and swiftly” after “troubling new revelations” were reported by The New York Times this week. 

The outlet reported on Wednesday that Democratic operatives and Peltola’s campaign were involved in an effort to recruit a second Dan Sullivan to run in the state’s Senate race.

“This new information has resulted in a significant surge of law enforcement assets to Alaska, and I have assigned several attorneys in my office to assist in the matter as well,” Heyman said. 

While the U.S. attorney would not disclose which potential crimes his office was looking into or who they were targeting in this investigation, he emphasized a commitment to election security. 

“What I can tell Alaskans is that we will not let anyone or any group undermine this election,” Heyman said. 

Peltola, the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee and the incumbent senator’s GOP challenger, Dan J. Sullivan, have all denied any involvement in the reported effort to recruit spoiler candidates for this race. 

“I just want to clear the air: I knew nothing about any other candidate on the ballot except for me and the incumbent,” Peltola said during a Thursday evening speech in Juneau, Alaska. “That is all I have ever known about. I am not interested in tricking voters.”

This week, President Trump called for both Peltola and the spoiler candidate to be removed from the ballot and prosecuted. Additionally, Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy (R) on Wednesday evening ordered an investigation into Peltola over The Times’s reporting. 

“Alaskans have a fundamental right to vote for the candidate they actually intend to support,” the Republican governor wrote on social media. “Deliberately tricking voters into casting their ballots for someone else strikes at the integrity of our elections.”

On Friday, Heyman urged anyone with knowledge about the “Dan Sullivan issue” or other potential election integrity violations to contact federal authorities. 

“Within the last 24 hours or so, we have received a number of new pieces of information that we’re following up on,” he said. “Anybody with additional information should contact the FBI as soon as possible.”

data.title: Cruz warns GOP could lose 8 Senate seats, get swept in Texas
data.description:
Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) is warning that Republicans could lose as many as eight Senate seats in the midterm election and get swept in all of the statewide Texas races, including the Senate contest between Republican Ken Paxton and Democrat James Talarico, if the GOP has a bad day on Nov. 3.

“The election is just a few days away and all across the country that are Senate races that are incredibly close. There are eight to 10 Senate races across the country that are basically tied,” Cruz said on a Friday episode of his podcast, “The Verdict with Ted Cruz.”

“If we have a good night on Election Day, we could have a fantastic result. We could end up with 53 Republicans in the Senate. We could end up growing our majority in the Senate,” he said.

But he warned “if we have a bad day” Republicans “could wake up the day after Election Day, instead of 53 Republicans, with 45.”

“That big a delta is at play,” Cruz said after traveling to Georgia, Texas, South Carolina, North Carolina, Michigan and Iowa to campaign for GOP candidates.

Cruz said there will be “massive Democratic turnout” in the midterm elections and warned that Republicans face a potential “blood bath” if Republicans don’t turn out to the polls in big numbers.

“I’m worried,” he said. “What we’re seeing across the country is massive Democrat turnout.

“Democrats are showing up, they’re energized, they hate, hate, hate Donald Trump,” he said. “If the election were over today, if just the early votes that have been cast so far are counted, Republicans would lose massively.”

But Cruz argued “there are Republican votes out there to turn that around” if GOP-leaning voters get motivated to vote.

He said reliable Democratic voters are showing up “in massive numbers.” But he said the reliable Republican voters aren’t voting early at the same rate as stalwart Democrats.

“Please, please, please show up and vote,” Cruz pleaded to his listeners.

He said there are more reliable Republican voters in the GOP-leaning Senate battleground states but they need to cast their ballots to make a difference.

Cruz warned that the statewide races in Texas are extremely close and warned that Republicans could get swept in the Lone Star State if things go wrong for their party.

“Texas is excruciatingly close. Understand we could lose Texas,” he warned. “Not just the Senate race. We could lose every single statewide race in Texas. That’s how close these numbers are.”

He countered Republicans who argue the polls are wrong by saying while pollsters may show left-leaning bias on occasion, the data showing huge Democratic turnout this year is very real.

“I can tell you having run a lot of campaigns, having examined a lot of numbers, these data are not fake. The Democrats are massively out-turning out the Republicans. We got to fix that.”

Cruz’s Senate office did not return a request for comment.

data.title: Treasury Department says Iran's economy cratering, inflation at 90 percent
data.description:
The U.S.’s economic isolation campaign against Iran is “decimating” the country’s economy, according to a Treasury Department report released Friday. 

The Trump administration launched its sweeping economic pressure campaign, dubbed Operation Economic Outcast, at the end of August. During a Wednesday appearance on CNBC, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the effort has been “very successful.”

The Treasury Department report found that Iran’s headline inflation, which measures the overall increase in prices across all goods and services in an economy, reached 90 percent in September after the operation was announced. 

Before the U.S. and Israel set off the conflict with joint strikes on Tehran at the end of February, headline inflation in Iran was sitting at around 70 percent. Core inflation, which excludes volatile items like food and energy, was just above 70 percent in September. 

“As the rial loses value and Iran’s access to international markets narrows, inflation is placing additional pressure on Iran’s already strained economy,” the report stated. “Rising prices are eroding purchasing power and increasing the cost of basic goods, while making it more expensive for Iran to obtain goods and inputs from abroad.”

The unofficial rial exchange rate hit 2,687,000 Iranian rials per U.S. dollar in October, according to the Treasury Department. 

The report also indicated that Tehran’s oil supplies have taken a hit amid U.S. sanctions and a months-long U.S. naval blockade in the Strait of Hormuz, a key oil trading corridor. 

The department said Iran has not loaded any oil onto vessels since Aug. 25, the day after Bessent announced Operation Economic Outcast. Iran is left with “nothing” after it sold its oil that was stranded at sea, according to the Treasury Department report. 

Iran’s aviation sector and formal financial sector have also been mired by the U.S.’s efforts to crush the country’s economy. The Treasury Department said it is also targeting “alternative channels” Iran has sought out to move money and skirt restrictions. 

“By identifying and disrupting cryptocurrency exchanges, wallets, financial facilitators, and other digital-asset infrastructure used to circumvent sanctions, Treasury is making it increasingly difficult for the regime to replace traditional financial channels with new ones,” the report stated. 

Critics of the Trump administration’s military and economic campaigns against Iran have pointed to domestic fiscal impacts, including the rising cost of fuel. The average price of a standard gallon of gas in the U.S. was up to $4.20 Friday afternoon, around a 38 percent increase from a year ago, according to AAA.

data.title: Trump says US looking into Binance hack: 'We don't know' if North Korea responsible
data.description:
President Trump said Friday his administration is looking into the $6.3 billion hacking of the cryptocurrency exchange Binance, the largest such hack on record.

“We don’t know,” Trump said in the Oval Office when asked if the hack should be attributed to a suspected North Korean hacker group.

“We’re looking at that,” he continued.

TraderTraitor, North Korea-based cybercrime group appears to be behind the Binance hacking, according to TRM Labs and Chainalysis, two blockchain intelligence firms.

The money began moving out of Binance wallets on Thursday afternoon. The company moved to suspend all deposits and withdrawals, while crypto firms froze some $3 billion in assets tied to the incident.

The attacker moved the money out of the wallets on XRP Ledger, Ethereum, Bitcoin, Tron, Solana and several other blockchain networks. Much of it occurred over a 20-minute span, TRM Labs said.

“It’s a hack,” Trump said. “That’s the problem. You know the old-fashioned way when you used to sign a check … these are different people, never see the money anymore. So I’ve always felt it was a little bit dangerous.”

“They say they have it pretty much under control,” he added. “We’ll see.”

TRM Labs noted that several aspects of the Binance hack match earlier North Korea-linked incidents, such as the $1.5 billion hack of crypto exchange Bybit last year.

Binance has said it will cover all the losses associated with the incident.

“Difficult times like this are a great reminder of how strong our industry is when we work together,” Binance co-CEO Richard Teng said in a video posted to the social platform X. “We are grateful to our partners that acted quickly to freeze their assets, to global law enforcement who we are working with hand-in-hand to seek justice.”

“But most of all, we are grateful to our users for their patience and understanding,” he continued. “Rest assured that we are working nonstop to resolve this, to make the users whole and live up to their trust.”

—Julia Shapero contributed to this report.
